title.rendered: Remi Tinubu and the Akara Economy

content.rendered:
Sometimes, a nation hears only what it wishes to hear. When the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, recently addressed journalists after meeting with governors’ wives on initiatives aimed at empowering local women, a short video clip quickly escaped its context and entered the unforgiving arena of social media. Before long, the conversation was no longer about women at the grassroots or economic empowerment. It became another political battleground. Her reference to businesses such as akara and kulikuli was interpreted by many as an insult to Nigerians struggling under severe economic hardship.

I watched the clip repeatedly. My conclusion differed from the popular outrage. She neither instructed unemployed graduates to abandon their ambitions nor suggested that frying akara should become national economic policy. Rather, she invoked something far more fundamental, which is the possibilities embedded in a small enterprise. Whether she articulated it perfectly is a different debate. What she described exists all around us, quietly sustaining millions of Nigerians who neither trend on social media nor dominate television panels. Most of the women she addresses are themselves existing in that informal economy, where livelihoods are built not on hashtags but on daily enterprise.

The tragedy of contemporary Nigeria is that we have become increasingly detached from the economy that actually feeds the country. Economists have long recognised the importance of small and medium-sized enterprises to national development. The World Bank has consistently identified SMEs as major drivers of employment and poverty reduction, particularly in developing economies. In Nigeria, millions of livelihoods are sustained outside air-conditioned offices and corporate boardrooms. They are found in cassava processing sheds, fish-smoking huts, tailoring workshops, mechanic villages, roadside food stalls, local dye pits and neighbourhood grinding mills. They may never make newspaper headlines, but together they constitute one of the most resilient foundations of the country’s economy.

Many of those loudly mocking the so-called “akara economy” today were themselves raised by it. Some were educated by mothers who woke before dawn to fry bean cakes. Others owe their university degrees to mothers who roasted corn by the roadside, or fathers who sold vegetables in village markets or traded in palm oil and garri. What appears insignificant from a distance has financed countless dreams. The contempt, therefore, is not for akara. It is for honest labour. There is something deeply unsettling about a society where people begin to believe they are bigger than work itself. Entitlement quietly replaces enterprise, and occupations become classified according to prestige rather than productivity. Sadly, economies do not grow because every citizen becomes a neurosurgeon, investment banker or artificial intelligence developer. They grow because millions of people create value, however modestly, every single day.

I have witnessed this truth repeatedly. Some years ago, I got to know a young Nigerian woman who had studied law in the United Kingdom.

Upon returning home, she made a decision many considered beneath her qualifications. She ventured into processing and selling goat and rabbit meat. Today, that modest beginning has grown into Tad Farms, a thriving enterprise with operations extending to Lagos and Abuja while exporting products to the United Kingdom and Canada. Her law degree did not become irrelevant; it became one of the intellectual tools she deployed in building a business instead of waiting endlessly for a juicy political job or a scarce white-collar job. Her story tells us that education is not diminished when it serves enterprise. Rather, enterprise is elevated when guided by education.

Closer to home is another story that has stayed with me for decades. Around 1998, an aunt of mine relocated with her husband from Agege to Sango-Ota. The community was expanding rapidly as new residential developments sprang up. Instead of lamenting the absence of white-collar opportunities, she observed the changing needs of her environment. Construction workers needed breakfast before heading to work each morning. She began by selling pap. Demand grew steadily, prompting her to add a grinding mill and later expand into the soft drinks business. Before long, she had built her own house. Today, she remains financially comfortable, not because fortune smiled on her unexpectedly, but because she recognised opportunity where others saw only routine. Neither her story nor that of the lawyer-turned-entrepreneur is extraordinary. That is precisely why both deserve attention. Across Nigeria, similar stories unfold quietly every day, beyond newspaper headlines and social media trends.

Ironically, many Nigerians who reject such occupations at home readily embrace them abroad. Graduates migrate to Europe and North America and begin life cleaning hospitals, caring for the elderly, washing dishes or working in warehouses. They perform these jobs with dignity because labour carries little social stigma in those societies. Yet some of the same individuals would reject comparable occupations in Nigeria, fearing ridicule more than poverty itself. That contradiction deserves honest reflection.

None of this is to deny Nigeria’s harsh economic realities. Hunger is real. Inflation has eroded purchasing power, and youth unemployment remains troubling. The government bears enormous responsibility for creating an environment in which businesses can survive, infrastructure functions efficiently, and investments flourish. Citizens cannot simply bootstrap their way out of structural economic failures. However, acknowledging governmental responsibility does not eliminate personal agency. The fight against unemployment will not be won by government recruitment alone. There are simply not enough white-collar jobs for the thousands of graduates produced annually. Sustainable employment will increasingly come through entrepreneurship, small businesses and expanding value chains.

Only recently, I visited Itoku in Abeokuta, the historic home of adire production. Behind the impressive Adire Mall lies another world: workshops where artisans painstakingly dye fabrics, carve intricate patterns and preserve one of Yorubaland’s oldest industries. There, I met a friend, a history graduate of the University of Ilorin who is completing a master’s degree on the history of adire while simultaneously building a business around it. Her journey itself attests to the fact that scholarship and entrepreneurship need not exist in separate worlds.

Equally fascinating was the story of one of her employees. The young man holds a National Diploma. His daily task involves stamping wax patterns onto fabrics, a job many graduates might dismiss because it stains the hands and clothes. Yet he earns about N10,000 on a productive day. Over a typical working month, that amounts to roughly N200,000, significantly more than the salaries earned by many university graduates employed in private schools for N45,000 or N50,000 monthly. The arithmetic is uncomfortable because it exposes a deeper problem. Too many Nigerians now measure work by appearance rather than by value. We celebrate certificates while overlooking productivity. We pursue status while neglecting wealth creation.

There is another warning embedded in this conversation. Some Asian countries have already become a major producer of textiles inspired by African designs, including adire — which my friend told me is common in Indonesia — fabrics now sold in Nigerian markets. If we continue despising indigenous enterprise while others industrialise it, we may eventually become importers of products that originated within our own cultural heritage. That would represent not only an economic failure but also a failure of imagination. Nations that prosper rarely despise the industries that spring naturally from their own soil.

The Yoruba have a saying: Olè l’ọba ọmọ jẹ — only stealing is disgraceful. Honest labour, regardless of its form, carries dignity. That proverb deserves renewed relevance in contemporary Nigeria. This is not an argument that every graduate should sell akara. It is an argument that no honest work should be considered beneath an educated person. Education should enlarge possibilities, not narrow them. Its highest purpose is not simply to produce job seekers but to nurture problem-solvers, innovators and creators of value.

Perhaps that is the lesson hidden beneath the political noise surrounding the First Lady’s remarks. The akara was never the story. The real story is whether Nigeria still possesses a culture that honours enterprise before entitlement, productivity before prestige and dignity before display. Unless we recover that culture, we will continue waiting for prosperity with hands that have forgotten the nobility of honest work.

The conversation does not end here. You can continue it with me on X via @folorunso_adisa, LinkedIn: Folorunso Fatai Adisa, or Facebook at Folorunso Fatai Adisa.
